edges.description: In the short-prodrome subset, organisms can be detected in cerebrospinal fluid and implicate direct central nervous system invasion.
In the longer-prodrome subset, respiratory infection elicits immune responses that injure central nervous system tissue after organisms are no longer demonstrable in cerebrospinal fluid.
In a rare acute-pneumonia branch, infection-associated vasculitis, hypercoagulability, and hypoperfusion can produce cerebral watershed infarction.
Acute respiratory infection triggers a systemic inflammatory response that commonly produces fever.
Organism entry into the central nervous system provides a direct route to inflammatory brain injury.
Neural autoantibody responses can produce inflammatory brain and deep gray matter injury after respiratory infection.
Occlusion of cerebral watershed territories directly manifests as focal cerebral infarction.
Brain inflammation downstream of M. pneumoniae infection manifests as infectious encephalitis.
In a lower-frequency cerebellar subset, M. pneumoniae-associated brain inflammation manifests with cerebellar ataxia.
Acute encephalitic brain inflammation commonly disturbs consciousness.
Encephalitic inflammation produces headache in most pediatric M. pneumoniae encephalitis cases.
Inflamed brain tissue can generate acute seizures and status epilepticus.
Central nervous system inflammation raises the cerebrospinal-fluid leukocyte count in an immune-mediated basal-ganglia subset.
Involvement of basal ganglia circuits can produce involuntary movement phenotypes in postinfectious M. pneumoniae-associated encephalitis.
Systemic inflammation downstream of infection drives fever.
